newsitem.title: USA: Hard-fought Teamsters election decided next week.
newsitem.headline: Hard-fought Teamsters election decided next week.

text.p: The hard-fought contest between Teamsters Union President Ron Carey and challenger James Hoffa entered its final week Wednesday as the two battled for control of the nation's second largest union.

The decision on whether Carey will be re-elected in the union's second open election ever or Hoffa will win the mantle once worn by his father Jimmy Hoffa has been in the hands of 1.4 million Teamster members for nearly a month. Next Tuesday, the staff of a court-appointed election officer begins counting ballots mailed in from across the country.

It is only the second election in the 93-year history of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters that has been open to all rank-and-file members. Before 1991, presidents of the union, known for years for labour corruption, were elected by convention delegates.
Government-supervised elections were required under a 1989 settlement of a federal racketeering suit.

Besides truckers and warehouse workers, the Teamsters represent flight attendants, public employees, miners, gravediggers and a wide range of workers in light industries like food processing, soft drinks, brewing and baking. Nearly one-third of its members are women.
Carey, 60, a former United Parcel Service driver and dissident leader of a New York local, won office five years ago in the first government-run election.

Hoffa, 55, whose father became a symbol of the union's corruption and was presumed murdered in 1975, is a labour lawyer who has worked for the past three years for a Teamsters joint council in Detroit that was once headed by his father.

Each candidate claims to be the real reformer in the race. Hoffa based much of his campaign on accusing Carey of being a government stooge who has ousted his political enemies under the guise of corruption-fighting and left the once wealthy union in a financial mess.
"This man has single-handedly brought the largest, richest union in the free world to the edge of bankruptcy," he said.
A key Hoffa campaign plank was to raise strike pay, in part by diverting $15 million from the union's general fund.

Carey blamed the union's financial woes on the lavish spending of his predecessors and a 1991 hike in strike pay that omitted an accompanying funding mechanism and drained the fund during a three-week national trucking strike in 1994.

He said he has ended years of deficit spending and declining membership, touted his anti-corruption record of putting more than 65 locals under temporary trusteeships and accused his opponent, whom he called "Junior," of being inexperienced and unfamiliar with unionism in the 1990s.
"His view is to go back to the weakness and corruption of the past," Carey said. "What we're doing is working."
Despite its newfound democracy, the 1.4 million member union cast only about 425,000 ballots in 1991, including more than 28,000 that were challenged or ruled ineligible.

With a week of balloting remaining, Hoffa spokesman Richard Leebove estimated that at least that many ballots already have been received. He predicted that turnout would be significantly higher than in 1991, especially in Hoffa's Midwest stronghold.
"We feel that that is a positive sign for us," he said.

Carey spokesman Steve Wattenmaker expected a turnout of 475,000 to 500,000 and said his camp was pleased with voter turnout in friendly locals. But making predictions can be risky since members often do not follow their leaders' endorsements, as the 1991 election showed, he said.
"In the privacy of their own homes, who knows how they'll vote?" Wattenmaker said.

The first voter tallies from a small number of locals might be available as early as Tuesday afternoon but both camps agreed a winner may not be declared until Dec. 13. The winner will begin his five-year term in January.
